# Discussion

```{r}
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

## Interpretation of Key Findings

This study set out to find out whether adding freeze-frame features to an xG model helps it predict whether a shot becomes a goal. A freeze frame is a snapshot of where the players were standing when the shot was taken, so it tells the model about the defenders and the goalkeeper and not just the shot itself. Before going through the findings, it is worth recalling how "better" was measured, because each measure looks at something different. The Brier score is the average squared gap between the predicted xG and what happened (1 for a goal, 0 for no goal), so a lower score means the probabilities were closer to reality. The AUROC is about ranking. It is the chance that a randomly chosen goal was given a higher xG than a randomly chosen non-goal, where 0.5 is no better than guessing and 1 is perfect. Log loss also scores the probabilities, but it punishes a model more heavily when it is very confident and wrong. The Brier skill score expresses the Brier score as an improvement over a model that gives every shot the overall goal rate, which makes it easier to see how much a model has really learned

The first main finding is that adding spatial features from the freeze-frame data improves xG predictions compared to a baseline that only describes the shot itself (Hypothesis 1). Adding the seven-literature standard spatial features to the baseline reduced the XGBoost Brier score from 0.0776 to 0.0737, a 5% improvement, lowered log loss from 0.2708 to 0.2578 and raised AUROC from 0,792 to 0.817. The improvement did not depend on the algorithm, since logistic regression showed the same pattern with its Brier score going from 0.0776 to 0.0747. This suggests that the freeze-frame features carry useful information in their own right, regardless of the type of model.

We also wanted to check that the freeze-frame features were adding something new, because the dataset already contains several event-context features. Some of these, such as whether a shot was a one-on-one, are filled in by the people collecting the data, who judge them by watching the match. They are one person's opinion about the same situation that the freeze frame records with coordinates. If the freeze-frame features were only repeating that opinion, adding them to a model that already had the event-context features should have changed very little. That is not what happened. Adding the event-context features alone lowered the Brier score by 3.4% (M1 to M3), and adding the freeze-frame features on top lowered it by a further 2.7% (M3 to M4). The reverse also held: adding the event-context features to the model with freeze-frame features (M2 to M4) lowered the Brier score by 1.0%. Each group of features therefore adds something beyond the other, and the freeze frame carries information that the annotators' judgements do not fully capture.

It is important to note that the improvements are small in absolute terms. The full XGBoost model (M5) reached a Brier score of 0.0728 compared with 0.0776 for the baseline, and the Brier skill score rose from 14.7% to 19.9%, which is about five percentage points. Part of the reason is that xG is a hard problem to improve upon. Only around 10% of shots are goals, and whether a shot goes in depends on a great deal that cannot be measured, such as the exact way the ball is struck or small deflections, so there is a limit to how well any model can do from positions alone. In xG models, significance is not the same as importance, as with 12,624 test shots, even tiny differences are statistically significant. Our model improvements may be significant, but that does not mean that the difference is big enough to matter. However, small improvements per shot can make a difference over the course of a season when the xG values of all shots get summed together [@decroos2020; @brechot2020], and so even a small improvement in model performance can still be useful.

The second finding is that the features mattered more than the algorithm. Going from M1 to M5 lowered the Brier score from 0.0776 to 0.0728 for XGBoost and from 0.0776 to 0.0731 for logistic regression, whereas XGBoost's advantage over logistic regression was never more than 1.3%. A logistic regression with good features did better than an XGBoost model with fewer features. For example, the M5 logistic regression (Brier 0.0731) outperformed the M2 XGBoost model (0.0737) and the M3 XGBoost model (0.0749). On the baseline features the two algorithms were identical, with a Brier score of 0.0776 for both. This makes sense, because there is little for a flexible model like XGBoost to find in just distance, angle, body part, assist type and play pattern that a logistic regression cannot already capture.

XGBoost was significantly better than logistic regression for M2 and M4, but not for M1, M3 or M5, and its advantage did not grow as more features were added. This only partly agrees with Robberechts and Davis [-@robberechts2020], who found that boosted trees did better than logistic regression once the feature set was richer. In addition, Tureen and Olthof [-@tureen2022] found that their Logistic Regression model outperformed XGBoost on 3 of 4 StatsBomb data splits. We cannot say for certain why we found less of a gap, but two explanations are plausible. The first is that the training set, about 49,000 shots of which roughly 10% are goals, may not contain enough goals for a flexible model to find much more than the main effects. The second is that XGBoost fitted the training data much more closely than the test data as features were added. For M5 its Brier score was 0.0679 on the training set and 0.0728 on the test set, while the M5 logistic regression scored 0.0741 on training and 0.0731 on test. This gap suggests XGBoost was partly learning noise in the training data, which is known as overfitting. Its test performance still did not get worse, and M5 XGBoost was the best model overall, so the overfitting limited the gains rather than damaging the results.

The third finding is that extending the spatial feature set did not help in a meaningful way. Adding the 20 extended spatial features to M4 moved the Brier score from 0.0729 to 0.0728, an improvement of 0.2%. The difference is detectable, with a p-value below 0.001, but it is far too small to matter in practice, so we do not consider Hypothesis 2 supported. Robberechts and Davis [-@robberechts2020] list a change in Brier less than or equal to 0.003 as negligible, and Bransen and Davis [-@bransen2021] considered models whose Brier scores differ by about 0.0005 to be similar. In our case the Brier difference is 0.0001, smaller than both. The practical question Hypothesis 2 asks is whether the extra engineering effort produces a meaningful improvement, and we conclude it did not.

This may look strange next to the SHAP results, because the extended spatial features account for 27.7% of the total SHAP importance in M5, and the two extended groups together account for 47.1%. SHAP is a method that shows how much each feature pushes the model's predictions up or down. The explanation is that importance and added value are not the same thing. When two features carry similar information, the model shares the credit between them, so a feature can look important even though the model could have gotten much of the same information from another one. The SHAP importance of `n_within_1m` is approximately 0 in M5 because it is strongly correlated with similar features describing the number of defenders in close proximity, but if those features were to be removed, the importance of `n_within_1m` may increase. The importance per feature supports this reading, since the extended features average about 1.1% of the total each, compared with about 4.4% for each of the literature-standard features. Agreement between the importance measures was also lower for M5 than for the smaller models, with a correlation of 0.73 between SHAP and permutation rankings compared with 0.87 to 1.00 for the others (@tbl-importance-agreement), which is what we would expect when many features overlap.

A few extended features did carry real weight. The proportion of the goal that is blocked (`goal_blocked`) was the third most important feature under all three importance measures. This is similar in spirit to one of the original features StatsBomb built from freeze frames, the proportion of the goal face that is blocked [@vatvani2022]. The fact that it adds so little to the Brier score despite ranking highly most likely reflects overlap with `DefendersInCone` and the other standard features, which already describe whether defenders are in the way.

The second research question asked which spatial features drive the improvement. In the spatial model (M2), shot angle was the most important feature by SHAP (0.57), followed by the distance between the shooter and the goalkeeper, `DistSGK` (0.43), then `DefendersInCone` (0.25) and the distance to the closest defender (0.19). In the full model (M5) `DistSGK` moved to the top at 0.50, just ahead of shot angle at 0.47. At first sight this suggests that goalkeeper features are the most important spatial group, with the defender and pressure features behind.

We are careful not to say this too strongly, because the evidence suggests `DistSGK` is partly a measure of distance to goal. Goalkeepers usually stand close to their own goal line, so the distance from the shooter to the keeper is very close to the distance from the shooter to the goal. Two results point to this. In XGBoost, the permutation importance of `DistToGoal` was only 0.9% once `DistSGK` was in the model, even though distance to goal is one of the most established predictors in the literature. Permutation importance measures how much worse the predictions get when a feature's values are shuffled at random, so a low value means the model could do without that feature. In the logistic regression the picture was reversed. `DistSGK` had no importance and a coefficient close to zero (odds ratio 0.996, p = 0.77), while `DistToGoal` ranked second, and the coefficients for `DistToGoal` (−0.085) and `DistToKeeper` (+0.079) were almost equal and opposite. That is what we would expect if the model was working out the shooter-to-keeper distance from those two features, which is roughly their difference. In the full model the logistic regression put most of its importance on `DistToGoal` (63.6% increase in Brier score when shuffled) and the shot's x location (19.2%), which again suggests several features were sharing the same information. The two algorithms therefore disagree about `DistSGK` on the surface, but they may be telling the same story in different ways. For this reason, we cannot give the goalkeeper's position all the credit, and the true contribution of goalkeeper features is probably smaller than the SHAP ranking suggests.

The direction of the effects is easier to interpret and mostly fits common sense. In the logistic regression, each additional defender in the shooting cone lowered the odds of a goal by about 26% (odds ratio 0.74), and a goalkeeper standing inside the shot triangle lowered the odds by about 33% (0.67). Each additional opponent within one metre of the shooter lowered the odds by about 21% (0.79), while a closest defender that was further away raised them (odds ratio 1.10 per unit of distance). The SHAP dependence plots tell the same story. Shots with no defenders in the cone had a positive effect on the prediction, shots with at least one defender had a negative effect that grew with each defender up to about four, and an open goal had a clearly positive effect. This matches Anzer and Bauer [-@anzer2021] who found the same pattern for defenders in the cone and goalkeeper position. The same pattern appears in the extended features, where the more of the goal that was blocked, and the more defenders close to the shooter and in the way, the lower the predicted chance, with a similar message from the density and pressure features.

Two results are less straightforward. The first is the effect of the goalkeeper's distance from their line (`DistToKeeper`). A keeper standing more than about 5 yards from goal was associated with a higher chance of scoring (odds ratio 1.08), which may seem backwards, since a keeper who comes out is meant to narrow the angle. We cannot tell the reason from this data, but one possibility is that a keeper who has left the line is more likely to be out of position, for example after a through ball or a dribble past a defender. The second is that the SHAP value for `DistSGK` peaks at about 5 yards and falls as the keeper gets closer to the shooter. One explanation is that a keeper right on top of the shooter is well placed to block or save the shot. Another is that when a keeper smothers the ball before a shot can be taken, no shot is recorded, so the shots that remain with the keeper very close may be unusual cases. The data cannot separate these two explanations, and this is discussed further in Section 6.3.

The third research question asks whether the improvement from spatial features varies by the location where the shot was taken. We found that the improvement from spatial features was larger inside the penalty box, which supports Hypothesis 3. The Spatial features lowered the Brier score by 5.5% for shots inside the box and by 2.3% for shots outside it (M1 to M2). With the Extended Baseline features already in the model, the improvements were 2.9% and 1.6% (M3 to M4). The Brier scores themselves are very different inside and outside the box (0.106 and 0.0319 for M1), because there are far more goals close to goal, so percentage improvements are the fairer way to compare the two. In addition, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test showed the difference between the zones was significant, with p-value less than 0.001 in @tbl-zone. The rank-sum test compares raw per-shot improvement, and inside shots start with bigger errors, leaving more room for improvement, further supporting the need to use the percentage comparison. When adding the Spatial and Extended Spatial features to the extended baseline (M3 to M5), we get the same result, with Brier improving by 3.1% inside the box compared to only 1.6% outside the box. Spatial information helps across the pitch, but it helps most close to goal. This fits the idea behind the hypothesis, because that is where defenders and the goalkeeper are closest to the shot and where small differences in their positions are most likely to change whether it goes in. However, AUROC improves equally both in and outside the box, and PR-AUC looks like shots outside improve more, but this may be only because PR-AUC is dependent on how often shots are goals, unlike AUROC. Very few goals are scored from outside the box. This is why PR-AUC for M1 XGB starts so low, with PR-AUC outside the box being only 0.14, as opposed to inside the box that starts with PR-AUC of 0.39. H3 is therefore supported.

Our models performed well against StatsBomb's own xG. The baseline models had a Brier score of 0.0776, which is around 5% worse than StatsBomb's 0.0736, and this gap is not surprising, because StatsBomb's model does not rely only on the standard features. It has used freeze-frame information from the start, including the number of blockers, the proportion of the goal that is blocked and an open-goal indicator, and since 2022 it has represented each defender as a smooth surface instead of a fixed circle [@vatvani2022]. The comparison is therefore between our models and another model that also uses spatial context. The first spatial model (M2 XGBoost, 0.0737) was roughly level with StatsBomb, and the full model (M5 XGBoost) had a Brier score 1.1% better (0.0728), which was statistically significant. M5 XGBoost also had a higher AUROC (0.825 compared with 0.820) and a lower log loss (0.2538 compared with 0.2573), as did M4 XGBoost, and the M5 logistic regression beat StatsBomb on both too. At the same time the predictions from our models were closely related to StatsBomb's, with correlations of 0.921 for M2 and 0.933 for M5. The biggest differences were for the best chances, where our model gave lower xG than StatsBomb to shots it rated above 0.75. Being roughly level with StatsBomb aligns with Scholtes and Karakuş [-@scholtes2024], who showed their baseline Brier was 0.086, and adding freeze-frame features lowered it to 0.076, while StatsBomb's was 0.075. This matches the same pattern of our models. Similarly, Hewitt and Karakuş's [-@hewitt2023] models correlated with StatsBomb xG with 0.887 and 0.902. Our correlations of 0.921 and 0.933 were even higher.

These margins are small and need careful reading. They only concern how accurate the probabilities are and how well shots are ranked. When xG was turned into a goal or no goal prediction using the goal-rate cut-off, StatsBomb still had the best accuracy, precision and F1 score, while our full model had the best recall. The significance tests are also not easy to line up with the sizes of the differences. For example, M4 XGBoost was 0.9% better than StatsBomb with a p-value of 0.54, while M4 logistic regression was only 0.1% better with a p-value below 0.001, which is partly because the test compares typical per-shot errors and not the average that the Brier score measures. The calibration plot shows that all our models were well calibrated, meaning that among shots given an xG of about 0.2, roughly 20% really were goals, while StatsBomb's xG sat slightly above the diagonal between about 0.1 and 0.35, meaning it somewhat underpredicted goals in that range. This same finding was made by Bajons and Harringer [-@bajons2025], who found the same calibration pattern.

Taken together, the results show that freeze-frame features give a modest but consistent improvement to xG predictions, that the improvement is similar for both algorithms, that it is largest close to goal, and that a small set of well-chosen features captures nearly all of it. The strongest evidence is that the improvement held in every comparison we made, with and without the event-context features, with both algorithms and in both areas of the pitch. The weakest areas are the attribution of the effect to particular features, because the distance measures overlap, and the size of the gains, which are small in absolute terms.

## Practical Applications

Beyond the statistical result that spatial features improve prediction (Hypothesis 1), the specific pattern of results in this study has several practical implications for how clubs and analysts might use a model like this one.

The first concerns player recruitment and performance evaluation. Clubs use xG to judge how good a player is at getting and finishing chances, and to help decide who to sign. A model that accounts for defender and goalkeeper positioning gives a fairer measure of finishing quality, since it does not credit a player for an easy shot or penalise a player for the defensive congestion they happened to shoot into. And since the improvement for any single shot is small, the benefit is more likely to show when xG is added up over many shots, such as across a season, than when judging one chance.

A model with good xG probabilities can be used practically to analyse player performance. @fig-xg-players below shows an example of a Premier League season, and each players number of goals scored against their xG, using StatsBomb xG values.

```{r}
#| label: fig-xg-players
#| fig-cap: "Goals scored against StatsBomb xG for players with 20 or more shots, Premier League 2015/16. Above the dashed line = more goals than their chances suggested. The three biggest over- and under-performers are labelled with randomly assigned IDs"
#| fig-scap: "Goals scored against StatsBomb xG for players with 20 or more shots, Premier League 2015/16"
#| fig-height: 5
season_players <- out("xg_season_players")
ggplot(season_players, aes(xg, goals, colour = role)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2.5) +
  geom_label_repel(data = bind_rows(slice_max(season_players, diff, n = 3), slice_min(season_players, diff, n = 3)),
                   aes(label = paste("Player", anon_id)), size = 3.2, seed = 1997, show.legend = FALSE,
                   fill = "white", label.size = 0, box.padding = 0.8, min.segment.length = 0,
                   nudge_x = c(-3, -3, -3, 3, 3, 3)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Defender = "#E69F00", Midfielder = "#009E73", Attacker = "#0072B2"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Expected goals (xG)", y = "Goals scored")
```

@fig-xg-players above shows that Player 101 was only expected to score about 17.7 goals, yet they scored 24. This player may have gotten very lucky that season, and would be expected to return to the mean in future seasons. Alternatively, a player who consistently overperforms their xG could be a sign that they indeed are a better goal scorer than those who underperform consistently. The same can be said about an entire team over or under performance. By looking at a team's expected goals and expected goals conceded each match over the course of season, you can derive a new statisitic called expected points. The probabilities of a win, draw, or loss are calculated from the xG of each team's shots across a match, and thus work out the expected points a team would earn for the match [@elhabr2022]. A high expected goal difference would result in an expected points value of close to 3, while a low expected goal difference would be close to 0. @fig-xg-season-points below shows the sum of all teams expected points during the 2015/2016 Premier League season, and plotted the expected points for the season against their actual points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-xg-season-points
#| fig-cap: "Actual points against expected points from StatsBomb xG, Premier League 2015/16. Above the dashed line = more points than their chances suggested"
#| fig-scap: "Actual points against expected points from StatsBomb xG, Premier League 2015/16"
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(out("xg_season_table"), aes(xpts, pts)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = team), size = 3.2, min.segment.length = 0, seed = 1997) +
  labs(x = "Expected points (from xG)", y = "Actual points")
```

@fig-xg-season-points above shows that Leicester City overperformed their expected points by over a dozen points. This could have been due to random chance, which is supported by the fact that this performance did not continue in the years after. Another use of xG is for predicting future team performance, as an alternative to merely looking at match outcomes. This is shown in @fig-xg-predicts below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-xg-predicts
#| fig-cap: "First-half-of-season goal difference and StatsBomb xG difference against second-half goal difference, Premier League, La Liga and Serie A 2015/16 (60 teams)"
#| fig-scap: "First-half goal and xG difference against second-half goal difference, 2015/16"
#| fig-height: 4.5
out("xg_halves") |>
  pivot_longer(c(xgd_first, gd_first), names_to = "predictor", values_to = "first_half") |>
  group_by(predictor) |>
  mutate(panel = paste0(if_else(predictor == "xgd_first", "First-half xG difference", "First-half goal difference"),
                        "\n(r = ", sprintf("%.2f", cor(first_half, gd_second)), ")")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(first_half, gd_second)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = comp), alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey30") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`La Liga` = "#E69F00", `Premier League` = "#0072B2", `Serie A` = "#009E73"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "First half of the season", y = "Second-half goal difference")
```

@fig-xg-predicts above shows that a team's expected goal difference over the first half of the season, is more highly correlated with their actual goal difference in the second half of the season, than their actual goal differences from the first half of the season. As goals are a rare event, match results are vulnerable to high variance, and xG allows us to slightly better predict how a team will continue to perform in the future than past form alone. Thus, by including spatial freeze-frame features in xG models, the resulting model may provide better xG values and probabilities, and thus they can be more reliably used to assess individual players, teams, and for predicting future performance.

The second implication follows from Hypothesis 3 that, the improvement from spatial features is concentrated inside the penalty box, where defensive congestion is highest, rather than being uniform across the pitch. This suggests that spatially adjusted xG is most valuable, and most trustworthy, for exactly the situations analysts care about most, such as player on player, while for shots from distance, where defensive positioning matters comparatively less, a simpler traditional model may be adequate. This also points to a secondary application where the same underlying freeze-frame features, especially those describing the goalkeeper's position relative to the shot, could be repurposed for goalkeeper-specific analysis, such as how well a keeper positions themselves regardless of whether a save was ultimately made.

The third implication concerns how much effort to put into building features. We've seen that extending the spatial feature set beyond the literature-standard variables (goalkeeper distance and angle, defender proximity) did not really produce a further meaningful improvement (a Brier score of 0.0729 became 0.0728). For a club or analyst, this suggests that most of the available benefit from freeze-frame data can be captured with a comparatively small set of spatial features, in a simple, easily explained model rather than requiring an extensive and costly custom engineering effort.

Finally, the fact that our best models matched or beat StatsBomb's own published xG on several measures despite being built entirely from open data and features engineered independently of StatsBomb's proprietary methodology, has a bigger implication for the accessibility of xG modelling. It suggests that clubs and analysts who want a model tailored to their specific league, or style of play can build a competitive in-house model rather than relying solely on a proprietary metric. This is consistent with the conclusion reached by Bajons and Harringer [-@bajons2025], that no single xG model suits every use, and that there is value in analysts being able to build and adapt their own.

## Limitations

### Pitch coordinates

As discussed in section 4.4.1, StatsBomb data standardises all location data into a 120 x 80 yard grid. As not all football pitches are the same size [@ifab2025], this results in slightly incorrect data, as the amount a coordinate gets scaled by depends on the size of the pitch the shot was taken on. This can be a problem when comparing data from many different matches, and as shown in Section 5.5.3, spatial context in the box, and small distances can be very important. We also grouped our data by zones, shots taken within and outside the box, but this grouping was done based on the standardised data. It is possible that shots were not taken from the same zone that their standardised coordinates would imply. It is also not clear whether StatsBomb maps coordinate relatively to the pitches painted lines, like the box, or if it is only relative to the edge of the pitch.

### Freeze-frame quality

A freeze frame only records the players visible to StatsBomb's camera system when the shot was taken. A defender who was on the pitch but outside the camera's field of view will simply be absent from the frame. This means that count-based features such as `DefendersInCone` and `DefendersBehindBall` are more accurately described as counts of visible defenders and are likely to understate the true number of players involved in a small but unknown proportion of shots. How complete the frames are have also changed over time. StatsBomb only began collecting freeze frames in 2018 [@hudl2021], so in our sample older frames contain fewer visible players. This means the count features cannot be compared exactly across years, and the effect of `DefendersInCone` may partly depend on how complete the frame was.

A freeze frame is also only a static snapshot. It shows where each player was standing at the instant of the shot, but nothing about their speed, direction of movement, or which way they were facing. Two defenders captured in the same position could be in very different defensive postures. One could be standing still on the goal side of the shooter, while the other is sprinting across to make a recovery run. The freeze frame cannot distinguish between them. This limits how much defensive context the freeze-frame-derived features can capture, regardless of how carefully they are engineered.

We also found 58 shots for which no goalkeeper could be identified in the freeze frame at all. Some of these are plausibly genuine data errors rather than a goalkeeper being truly absent, but we cannot verify this with certainty, and if the goalkeeper has been mislabelled or omitted, we cannot be confident that the remaining players in that same frame are labelled correctly either.

### What counts as a shot

This study only models shots that were actually taken and recorded as shot events. It cannot see situations where a defender or goalkeeper's positioning was very effective that no shot was ever attempted. For example, a goalkeeper rushing out to smother the ball at a striker's feet before a shot can be taken. These situations are, in a real sense, the most extreme possible case of good goalkeeper positioning reducing a team's chances of scoring, yet they are invisible to a shot-based model by construction. This could help explain why the effect of `DistSGK` drops when the keeper is very close to the shooter.

We also observed an inconsistency in how set-piece situations are logged as shot events. A corner kick appears to be recorded as a shot event only when the resulting effort is on target, while corners that are blocked, off target, or otherwise do not test the goalkeeper are instead logged as pass events. A similar pattern may apply to free kicks taken near the byline that are effectively deep crosses rather than direct efforts on goal. This means the small number of corner shots in our sample (19) likely understates genuine corner-kick shooting opportunities, rather than reflecting how rarely teams shoot directly from corners. This is one reason corners and direct free kicks were excluded (Section 1.3). Together with the exclusion of penalties, it means the study says nothing about shot quality from set pieces, and its findings apply only to open play shots.

### Sample

The StatsBomb open data is not a random sample of football matches. It reflects whichever leagues, seasons, and competitions StatsBomb has chosen to make publicly available, and some of these are represented far more heavily than others. In particular, the 2015/16 season of the top five European leagues alone contributes 38,361 shots, or roughly 58% of the entire sample used in this study. This means that, despite the dataset nominally spanning many decades and competitions, our results are disproportionately shaped by the shooting patterns, tactics, and data recording of that one season, and should not be assumed to generalise evenly across the other years and competitions.

Finally, as discussed in Section 1.3, this study is also restricted to men's competitions. Prior work has shown that shot outcomes and feature importance can differ meaningfully between men's and women's football [@bransen2021]. Our findings should therefore not be assumed to hold for women's football without separate validation.

### StatsBomb's xG

StatsBomb's proprietary model is trained on a far larger pool of shots than are available in the open data used here, covering many more competitions and seasons, and it may use additional proprietary features that are not published and that we have no way of replicating. Our model being close to, and in some measures ahead of, StatsBomb's xG should therefore be read as a good result given a much smaller and more limited dataset, rather than as a strictly fair contest between two models built under the same conditions.

### Excluded information and observations

As noted in the Methodology chapter, we excluded any feature that can only be known after a shot's outcome is already determined such as, average shot velocity, and any events that only occur after the shot is taken (blocks and saves). We did this to avoid data leakage. This is a necessary safeguard, but it is also a limitation as these excluded variables may carry real predictive information that our models could not use. We also removed 65 shots that took place off camera, because their player positions are estimates, 58 shots with no goalkeeper in the freeze frame, and 119 shots with other missing features.

### Statistical tests and importance measures

The significance tests used in this study treat each shot as separate from the others. However, in reality, shots from the same match share things like team strength, tactics and conditions, so they are related to each other. This probably makes the p-values smaller than they should be, which is another reason a very small p-value should be read as showing a difference is detectable and not that it is large. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test we used also compares the typical, or median, per-shot squared error, whereas the Brier score is the average. When about 90% of shots are non-goals and have very small errors, the two can behave differently, which is why some p-values do not line up neatly with the sizes of the Brier differences.

The importance measures also have limits when features overlap. SHAP and permutation importance both split or hide credit between similar features, as the `DistSGK` and `DistToGoal` results show, so the rankings should be read as a guide and not as exact measurements of each feature's contribution.

## Recommended Extensions to Research

There are several next steps. The most direct is to repeat the analysis using only the years in which freeze frames are most complete, or to compare results across years, to see whether the effect of count features such as `DefendersInCone` depends on how many players are captured in the frame.

A second is to use confidence intervals from a bootstrap that resamples whole matches, or models that allow for differences between matches, teams and players. This would give more reliable measures of uncertainty and help separate a player's finishing skill from the quality of the chances they get.

Testing our second hypothesis showed that adding the extended spatial features (M4 to M5) resulted in a very small improvement in Brier score, and that SHAP importance credit is split across highly correlated features. A smaller model using only the most important of all the spatial features, such as `DefendersInCone`, `gk_in_triangle`, and `goal_blocked`, may perform as well as M5 while being a simpler, and thus more interpretable model. In addition, the inclusion of monotonic constraints [@vatvani2022] can make xG changes more sensible and smooth, and may further improve interpretability, as they would force features to be used in a way that better reflects reality. For example, we know that the further from the goal, and the tighter the angle, the harder it is to score, all else being equal.

Another extension is creating a full xG model for all types of shots, as we only looked at shots from open play. This could be done by using different models for different kinds of shots, such as what was done by Anzer and Bauer [-@anzer2021], who used a combination of separate sub-models. Our H3 results showed that there is a difference between shots in and outside the box, and thus modelling them separately may result in more interpretable results relevant to each situation. The same could be said for shots taken with the foot as opposed to a header both in and out the box, or headers from open play as opposed to a set piece.

It is possible to add additional features of a wide variety, but an interesting extension of our research would be to add more advanced features that look at event data prior to the goal. We used some like key passes, but there is much more one could do with a wealth of match event data. It would then be interesting to look at the freeze-frame data from the other match events, to create new spatial features, and to test if freeze-frame context improves models even when those freeze-frames aren't from only the shot event.

Other extensions concern the data. Tracking data that includes player speed and direction would address the still-picture problem, because it could separate a defender who is standing still from one who is running into position. Separate models for men's and women's football, or a model that includes gender as a feature, would show whether the spatial effects carry over to the women's game. Testing on later seasons than those used for training would be a harder check of how well the models generalise than a random split of matches. Finally, set pieces could be modelled once they are logged consistently, and the freeze-frame features could be used for goalkeeper-focused analysis.
